title: Kestrel AI - VDB fallback, embedding dims & deployment options
summary: Discovery call to understand Kestrel's retrieval/rerank scale and constraints. Key concerns: embedding size tradeoffs (128 vs 512), vector DB cold-start and fallback behavior, private/VPC requirements for sensitive data, and benchmark plan for throughput and tail latency. Redwood AE and SE outlined hosted/dedicated/private options and proposed a pilot with an eval spreadsheet and a 2-week benchmark run.
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark template and cost estimate (Maya) - due 2026-08-18
Schedule SE deep-dive to map current infra and run sample queries (Tom + Kestrel team) - tentative 2026-08-20
Customer to provide sample dataset (10k docs) and current embedding config - Kestrel
action_items: Maya Chen: Send pilot SOW and benchmark template (due 2026-08-18)
Tom Alvarez: Set up initial benchmark run and provide RBAC checklist for VPC (due 2026-08-21)
Asha Patel: Upload 10k doc sample and current pipeline snippet to shared drive (no later than 2026-08-19)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-15 15:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Tom Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Reddy (Kestrel Head of Search), Marco Silva (Eng Manager), Asha Patel (Data Eng)
Links shared: redwood.com/security/soc2 (link), benchmark-template.xlsx (shared), pilot-sow-draft.pdf (shared)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hi everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick agenda — understand your retrieval/rerank throughput needs, deployment constraints, and next steps for a pilot.
[00:18] Priya Reddy: thanks, maya. overview from our side — Kestrel's search powers a few customer-facing apps, we do a two-stage retrieval: ANN from our vector DB then a reranker using a 7B model. We're hitting tail latency and costs as queries scale.
[00:35] Marco Silva: and we run in GCP, currently using a managed vector store, but we've seen cold start spikes and some availability issues. looking at options: keep hosted vector DB + host model inference elsewhere, or move vector store on-prem.
[00:50] Tom Alvarez: okay, makes sense. can you give ballpark qps and P95 targets?
[01:02] Priya Reddy: baseline is 150 qps during peak windows, we'd like P95 under 150ms for retrieval+rerank combined if possible. realistic target maybe 200ms.
[01:18] Maya Chen: good — that's helpful. one immediate tradeoff we usually discuss is embedding dimensionality. higher dims like 512 usually give better recall but cost more in storage and vector DB query time. have you benchmarked 128 vs 256 vs 512?
[01:36] Asha Patel: we've been using 768 dims from our existing embedder, but that's painful. storage and cosine lookups are heavy. we want to try reducing dims.
[01:46] Marco Silva: right now we do 768 -> we compress with PCA to 256 for index, but the production pipeline still carries 768 sometimes.
[02:01] Tom Alvarez: that pattern's common. if you can accept a small recall delta, 256 is a big win for throughput. also consider hybrid rerank: do lightweight retrieval at 256 then rerank with context windows to recover precision.
[02:18] Priya Reddy: what's the impact on tail latency if we move to 256?
[02:24] Tom Alvarez: it's nonlinear — index memory footprint drops so more of it stays in memory, reducing disk IO and tail spikes. for Pinecone-like managed stores we've seen P95 drop 20-40% when moving 768->256 for same shard counts. caveat: depends on your similarity metric and sharding.
[02:44] Priya Reddy: ok. another concern: vector DB fallback and availability. when the ANN service degrades, we need graceful fallback to a cheaper index or to Redwood-hosted nearest neighbors without dropping queries. how does Redwood handle routing/fallback?
[03:03] Maya Chen: good question. Redwood can do smart routing — you can keep your primary ANN and configure a fallback policy to route to a hosted approximate index or a no-ANN low-latency path that uses cached top-k results. for Dedicated we also support co-located indexing if you want determinism. the fallback can be configured by latency, error rate, or explicit health checks.
[03:28] Marco Silva: is that built into the runtime or is it an optional orchestration layer we have to manage?
[03:34] Tom Alvarez: built into the orchestration layer. runtime exposes health signals and the control plane can switch traffic. for private/VPC deployments we give you control plane hooks so you can own the health checks. one thing to watch: fallbacks that switch to higher-latency rerank models can increase cost — we usually recommend a circuit-breaker style threshold and a short-term cache for the top-K rerank outputs.
[03:59] Asha Patel: when you say "hosted approximate index" — is Redwood running a separate index or are you referencing an integrated vector DB?
[04:08] Maya Chen: currently Redwood doesn't replace all vector DB functionality, but we offer an optional lightweight embed-index service for fallback and caching; for production-scale stores, we integrate with your vector DB (we have connectors for Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate, Elasticsearch). fallback index is meant for short windows and reduces cold-start impact.
[04:28] Priya Reddy: security is big for us — we need SOC2, SSO, KMS for encryption at rest, and VPC peering for Private deployments. can you run through the differences between Hosted, Dedicated and Private for data residency?
[04:44] Maya Chen: sure. Hosted has the fastest onboarding — data processed in Redwood tenancy, SOC2 certed, but not for sensitive PII unless you opt in to dedicated. Dedicated gives reserved capacity in our tenancy, with stronger isolation and customer-specific routing. Private (VPC or on-prem) means the inference runtime sits in your VPC, keys never leave your network, and we integrate with your KMS/HSM. all three can provide audit logs; Private adds the most control for compliance.
[05:12] Marco Silva: would Private still allow Redwood Console observability?
[05:17] Tom Alvarez: yes, with a control-plane link that surfaces metrics; logs can be pushed to your storage, or we can mirror only non-sensitive telemetry. it's configurable.
[05:27] Priya Reddy: ok that's promising. on costs — at what point does Dedicated make sense over Hosted?
[05:33] Maya Chen: typically when sustained throughput and predictable SLOs matter. if you have steady >100K inference tokens/day or heavy rerank workloads causing unpredictable throttling, Dedicated can lower unit cost by 20-40% depending on commit. but we'll model your workload in the benchmark.
[05:50] Marco Silva: let's talk benchmarks — what do you need from us to run a representative test?
[05:56] Tom Alvarez: sample dataset of ~10k documents, representative queries (50-100 query templates), and your current embedding pipeline code + index config. we'll run parallel runs: your current vector DB baseline, Redwood-hosted (with fallback enabled), and Dedicated-configured scenarios. measure cold-start P95, steady-state P95, and cost per 1000 queries.
[06:19] Priya Reddy: how long does a benchmark take?
[06:22] Tom Alvarez: typically 3-7 days for initial runs, then tune for another week. for your case we can aim for a 2-week pilot including tuning.
[06:30] Maya Chen: action items — we'll send the benchmark template and SOW. Tom will set up a meet to review infra access patterns and any VPC needs.
[06:40] Asha Patel: quick question — are there quantized model options for rerank that still give good quality?
[06:46] Tom Alvarez: yes, we support int8 and some int4 paths depending on model architecture; for rerank we often use int8 with calibration to preserve score ordering. quality regressions are measured against your eval set during the pilot.
[07:02] Marco Silva: competitor question — if we already use Pinecone, what's Redwood's win?
[07:07] Maya Chen: Redwood is inference-first — we couple model serving, KV cache, batching, and routing policies. so you don't have to stitch a separate low-latency inference layer, fallback logic, and rollout controls. we focus on predictable SLOs and cost levers like batching and quantization.
[07:24] Priya Reddy: alright, that covers high level. can you send a proposed pilot timeline and estimated costs?
[07:29] Maya Chen: yes — we'll send SOW and a cost estimate by Tue 2026-08-18.
[07:34] Marco Silva: ok thanks.
[07:36] Maya Chen: any final questions?
[07:38] Priya Reddy: none from me. excited to see the benchmark.
[07:41] Asha Patel: I'll get the dataset uploaded.
[07:43] Tom Alvarez: we'll follow up with calendar invites for the deep-dive.
[07:47] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with next steps.

End of meeting.
Notes on transcription: occasional mishears ("K-F cache" for KV cache), names sometimes condensed.
